title: Jammu Police Seize 20 Bags of Suspected Adulterated Paneer From Bus
excerpt: Officers intercepted the bus at Greater Kailash Naka and handed the consignment to the Food Safety Department for testing, the latest bust in the Union Territory's running crackdown on fake dairy.
body:
• Jammu Police intercepted a passenger bus (registration JK02CE-4300) at Greater Kailash Naka on September 15 and seized 20 bags of paneer suspected of being adulterated.
  • The consignment was handed over to the Food Safety Department for examination and sampling; further legal proceedings under the Food Safety and Standards Act will follow the lab results.
  • The seizure adds to a string of dairy busts in the region, including 16 quintals pulled off two buses in Samba last September.
  • Jammu and Kashmir has banned the manufacture, sale and transport of loose paneer containing foreign or vegetable fat after laboratory tests confirmed adulteration.

Bus Stopped During Routine Checking

Jammu Police intercepted a passenger bus at Greater Kailash Naka on September 15 and seized 20 bags of paneer suspected to be adulterated, officials said. The bus, bearing registration number JK02CE-4300, was stopped during checking within the jurisdiction of Police Station Gangyal, where officers found the suspected dairy product being transported in the vehicle.

Police informed the Food Safety Department and called its officials to the Gangyal police station for further action. The recovered paneer was handed over to the department for examination and sampling. Further proceedings will be initiated by the department under the applicable legal provisions based on the results.

A Long-Running Crackdown on Fake Dairy

This is not an isolated haul. Jammu and Kashmir has been fighting a sustained battle against adulterated paneer moving through its transport corridors. In September 2025, Samba Police seized roughly 16 quintals of adulterated paneer from two passenger buses, one arriving from Amritsar and the other from Delhi; on-the-spot sampling found the product adulterated with vanaspati oil and unfit for human consumption. Earlier busts include 11 quintals recovered from an auto at the Jammu bus stand and a consignment of suspected synthetic paneer found during routine patrolling at the New Bus Stand in August 2025.

The pattern is consistent: paneer manufactured outside the Union Territory, moved in passenger buses and private vehicles without refrigeration, invoices or warranty declarations, and pushed into local dairy shops and markets. Tests at the National Food Laboratory in Ghaziabad have repeatedly found beta-sitosterol in seized samples, a marker of vegetable or foreign fat that has no place in paneer under the Food Safety and Standards (Food Products Standards and Food Additives) Regulations, 2011.

In response, the administration prohibited the manufacture, sale, distribution, import and transportation of loose paneer containing foreign fat across the Union Territory under Section 30(2)(a) of the Food Safety and Standards Act, 2006. Similar enforcement drives have been reported in other states, including Haryana and Telangana, where authorities have moved against fake and analogue paneer.

Impact & Analysis

The enforcement logic is straightforward: intercept the supply chain before the product reaches retail. Passenger buses have become a preferred courier for the trade precisely because they blend into daily traffic at checkpoints, and the repeated seizures suggest the economics still work for the suppliers despite the risk. For consumers, the danger is invisible at the point of purchase. Adulterated paneer looks and cooks like the real thing; only laboratory analysis reveals the substituted fats.

"The loose paneer consignments containing foreign fat and without any traceability pose a serious risk to public health."

— Smita Sethi, Commissioner of Food Safety, Jammu and Kashmir, in the prohibitory order

Diaspora Angle

Paneer is a staple in vegetarian Indian kitchens, and the scale of the fake-paneer trade is a practical reason for diaspora families to buy dairy only from established, FSSAI-licensed brands when in India, and to check labels and sourcing when buying paneer abroad.

What’s Next

The Food Safety Department’s examination and sampling of the seized 20 bags will determine whether prosecution follows under the Food Safety and Standards Act. The seizure also lands in the middle of a wider enforcement push: Chief Minister Omar Abdullah has ordered exemplary punitive action against food-safety violators, backed by a 30-day action plan that includes intensified inspection drives across all districts, food testing labs at every district headquarters, entry check posts at Lakhanpur and Qazigund, and a “Dial 104” public reporting line for unsafe food.
